## Classes

### <a name="windowspowershell"></a>`windowspowershell`

This class owns every *site-wide* path and setting. It does **not** own an
in-house module identity any more: a site can build as many in-house
modules as it wants, each declared with `windowspowershell::module`
(title = the module name) and populated with
`windowspowershell::script { ... modulename => '<that title>' }`. There is
no module-wide default module name: each `windowspowershell::script` has to
say which in-house module it belongs to.

On a non-Windows node the whole module is a no-op, including both defined
types, so it is safe to classify nodes without filtering on the operating
system.

#### Examples

##### Build an in-house module and deploy a script into it

```puppet
include windowspowershell

windowspowershell::module { 'Acme':
  version     => '1.2',
  companyname => 'Acme Corp',
  author      => 'Platform Team',
}

windowspowershell::script { 'Get-DiskUsage':
  modulename => 'Acme',
  content    => file('profile/powershell/Get-DiskUsage.ps1'),
}
```

##### Install through an authenticating proxy

```puppet
class { 'windowspowershell':
  proxy            => 'http://proxy.example.net:3128',
  proxy_credential => {
    username => 'svc-puppet',
    password => Sensitive('s3cret'),
  },
}
```

##### Deploy a third-party module

```puppet
windowspowershell::external_module { 'PSWindowsUpdate':
  ensure     => '2.2.1.5',
  repository => 'PSGallery',
}
```

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--module_root"></a>`module_root`

Data type: `Windowspowershell::Rootpath`

Machine-wide PowerShell module directory, shared by every in-house module
this class lays out and by `windowspowershell::external_module`. The module manages this directory itself (via ensure_resource,
so it can be co-managed by another module), but its parent must already
exist.

Default value: `'C:\Program Files\WindowsPowerShell\Modules'`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--manage_profiles"></a>`manage_profiles`

Data type: `Boolean`

Whether to manage the machine-wide PowerShell profiles. Each in-house
module with `import_in_profile => true` (the default) adds its own
`Import-Module` line to these profiles; `windowspowershell::external_module` does
the same for a third-party module when `import_in_profile => true` is
passed to it.
The profile files are owned by Puppet: on every run, anything in them that
does not come from a `concat::fragment` targeting them is removed. Other
Puppet code can add its own content by declaring a `concat::fragment` with
`target` set to a path in `$windowspowershell::profile_paths` and an
`order` between `01` and `49` (before the module imports) or `70` and `99`
(after them); `00` is the header, `50` the in-house imports and `60` the
external imports. Lines added by a GPO startup script or by hand are not
preserved. See "Co-managing the profiles" in the README.

Default value: `true`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--manage_pwsh_profile"></a>`manage_pwsh_profile`

Data type: `Optional[Boolean]`

Whether to manage the PowerShell 7 profile. Left `undef`, it is managed
only on nodes where PowerShell 7 is installed at its default location
(`C:\Program Files\PowerShell\7\pwsh.exe`); a ZIP, Microsoft Store or
32-bit install elsewhere is not detected. Set it in Hiera to opt a
whole agent environment in or out.

Default value: `undef`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--proxy"></a>`proxy`

Data type: `Optional[Windowspowershell::Proxyurl]`

Proxy passed to `Install-Module` when installing a third-party module from
a repository. Left `undef`, no proxy is used and installs go out directly.
Set it to an explicit proxy URL (e.g. 'http://proxy.example.net:3128').
Credentials embedded in the URL (`http://user:pass@host`) are still
accepted for now but deprecated: they end up in clear text in the Exec
command, and .NET may not honor them. Use `proxy_credential` instead.

Default value: `undef`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--proxy_credential"></a>`proxy_credential`

Data type:

```puppet
Optional[Struct[{
        username => String[1],
        password => Sensitive[String[1]],
  }]]
```

Credentials for an authenticating proxy, as a hash with `username` and a
`Sensitive` `password`. Requires `proxy`, and is mutually exclusive with
credentials embedded in the `proxy` URL. They are passed to
`Install-Module` and `Install-PackageProvider` through `-ProxyCredential`;
the secret travels in the Exec `environment` (redacted from reports and
logs) and never appears in the Exec `command` or `unless` text.

Default value: `undef`

## Defined types

### <a name="windowspowershell--external_module"></a>`windowspowershell::external_module`

One resource manages one module, not one version, so `ensure` carries the
version the way it does on the `package` type. By default every other version
found side by side is removed, which is what makes a single resource enough
to express "this node runs 2.2.1.5 and nothing else".

This is separate from `windowspowershell::script`: a third-party module ships
its own manifest, so it takes no part in regenerating the in-house one.

#### Examples

##### Pin a version from the PowerShell Gallery

```puppet
windowspowershell::external_module { 'PSWindowsUpdate':
  ensure     => '2.2.1.5',
  repository => 'PSGallery',
}
```

##### Copy the files from a Puppet source instead

```puppet
windowspowershell::external_module { 'PSWindowsUpdate':
  ensure => '2.2.1.5',
  source => 'puppet:///modules/windowsupdate/PSWindowsUpdate/2.2.1.5/',
}
```

##### Remove a module entirely

```puppet
windowspowershell::external_module { 'PSWindowsUpdate':
  ensure => absent,
}
```

#### Parameters

The following parameters are available in the `windowspowershell::external_module` defined type:

* [`ensure`](#-windowspowershell--external_module--ensure)
* [`modulename`](#-windowspowershell--external_module--modulename)
* [`repository`](#-windowspowershell--external_module--repository)
* [`source`](#-windowspowershell--external_module--source)
* [`purge_versions`](#-windowspowershell--external_module--purge_versions)
* [`import_in_profile`](#-windowspowershell--external_module--import_in_profile)

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--external_module--ensure"></a>`ensure`

Data type: `Windowspowershell::Externalmoduleensure`

`absent` removes every version installed under the machine-wide (`AllUsers`)
module directory and unregisters the module from PowerShellGet. `present`
accepts any version and installs the newest one if none is there, which
requires `repository`. It is install-once: once any version is present it is
never upgraded on later runs. To move a node to a newer version, pin that
version in `ensure`.
A version string pins that exact version. PowerShellGet may normalise a
short pin into a longer folder name (e.g. pin `2.1` installs under
`2.1.0`); that normalised folder counts as the pinned version, so the
install check stays idempotent and the purge keeps it.

Default value: `'present'`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--external_module--modulename"></a>`modulename`

Data type: `Windowspowershell::Name`

Name of the PowerShell module. Defaults to the resource title.
Declare one resource per `modulename`: two resources sharing a
`modulename` under different titles each purge the other side's version
(see `purge_versions`), so the node flaps between both versions and never
converges. Sharing is only supported with `purge_versions => false` on all
but one side, and only with the `repository` backend: with the `source`
backend both titles declare the same versioned `File` directory, which
fails the catalogue with a duplicate resource.

Default value: `$name`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--external_module--repository"></a>`repository`

Data type: `Optional[Windowspowershell::Reponame]`

Repository to install from, e.g. `PSGallery`. Mutually exclusive with
`source`. The install runs with `-Force -AllowClobber` as `SYSTEM`, which
suppresses the untrusted-repository prompt: the repository named here is
trusted to execute code as `SYSTEM`, so prefer an internal mirror in
production.

Default value: `undef`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--external_module--source"></a>`source`

Data type: `Optional[String[1]]`

Puppet file source holding the module files, for nodes that cannot reach a
repository. Mutually exclusive with `repository`.

Default value: `undef`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--external_module--purge_versions"></a>`purge_versions`

Data type: `Boolean`

Whether to remove versions of the module other than the one in `ensure`.
Ignored unless `ensure` is a version. Co-managing one modulename from both
`windowspowershell::external_module` and `windowspowershell::module`
requires `purge_versions => false` on one side, or each purge removes the
other side's version. The same holds for two `external_module` resources
sharing a `modulename`: keep a single resource per module, or set
`purge_versions => false` on all but one side when the sharing is
deliberate.
Comparison is numeric with missing segments treated as zero, so pin `2.1`
also matches folder `2.1.0`: if both spellings end up side by side, both
count as the pinned version and neither is purged. The canonical folder
is whatever the backend creates -- the normalised name PowerShellGet
picks for `repository`, the literal pin for `source` -- so remove the
other spelling once by hand if it ever appears.

Default value: `true`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--external_module--import_in_profile"></a>`import_in_profile`

Data type: `Boolean`

Whether to add an `Import-Module` line for this module to every profile
file managed by `windowspowershell::config` (see `manage_profiles` /
`manage_pwsh_profile` on the main class). Pins `-RequiredVersion` when
`ensure` is a specific version. Ignored (no-op) when `ensure => absent`.
A single-component pin such as `2` is normalised to `2.0` for the
`-RequiredVersion` line, because `Import-Module -RequiredVersion` is
typed `[version]` and needs at least major.minor.

Default value: `false`

### <a name="windowspowershell--module"></a>`windowspowershell::module`

One resource is one module identity: its manifest (`.psd1`) is regenerated
by a shared, refresh-only `Exec`, namespaced to this module's name, that
every `windowspowershell::script { ..., modulename => <this title> }`
notifies. A site that needs several in-house modules declares one
`windowspowershell::module` per module name; nothing here is a
module-wide singleton any more.

A `windowspowershell::script` that names a module which was never declared
explicitly gets one with every default, via `ensure_resource`. Declare this
resource explicitly only when a default (`version`, `companyname` or
`author`) needs overriding -- in which case it must be declared before the
first `windowspowershell::script` that names it, since `ensure_resource`
only fills in the gap when nothing has claimed the title yet.

The resource title is the in-house module name: this is the value every
`windowspowershell::script` must pass as its own `modulename` to land its
scripts here. Unlike `windowspowershell::external_module` (third-party, where several
resource titles may legitimately share a target module), one
`windowspowershell::module` resource is the one and only build of
that module identity: the manifest, the root module file and the Functions
directory are singletons, so declaring the same module name twice is a
genuine conflict and fails to compile like any other duplicate resource
declaration, rather than being silently merged.

#### Examples

##### Declare a module with non-default identity, then deploy scripts into it

```puppet
windowspowershell::module { 'Acme':
  version     => '1.2',
  companyname => 'Acme Corp',
  author      => 'Platform Team',
}

windowspowershell::script { 'Get-DiskUsage':
  modulename => 'Acme',
  content    => file('profile/powershell/Get-DiskUsage.ps1'),
}
```

##### Build a module dynamically from a whole directory of scripts

```puppet
windowspowershell::module { 'Acme':
  source => 'puppet:///modules/profile/acme-scripts',
}
```

#### Parameters

The following parameters are available in the `windowspowershell::module` defined type:

* [`version`](#-windowspowershell--module--version)
* [`companyname`](#-windowspowershell--module--companyname)
* [`author`](#-windowspowershell--module--author)
* [`import_in_profile`](#-windowspowershell--module--import_in_profile)
* [`source`](#-windowspowershell--module--source)
* [`purge_versions`](#-windowspowershell--module--purge_versions)

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--module--version"></a>`version`

Data type: `Windowspowershell::Moduleversion`

Version folder the module is installed under, and the ModuleVersion written
into the generated manifest. Defaults to `1.0`. Requires at least two
dot-separated components: a single number such as `1` is rejected at compile
time because PowerShell's `[version]` type, which `-ModuleVersion` casts to,
requires both a major and a minor version.

Default value: `'1.0'`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--module--companyname"></a>`companyname`

Data type: `Windowspowershell::Psstring`

CompanyName field written into the generated module manifest. Defaults to
the neutral `Unknown`; override with the real company.

Default value: `'Unknown'`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--module--author"></a>`author`

Data type: `Windowspowershell::Psstring`

Author field written into the generated module manifest. Defaults to the
neutral `Unknown`; a team or service identity is a better fit than a
person's name, since it stays meaningful over time.

Default value: `'Unknown'`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--module--import_in_profile"></a>`import_in_profile`

Data type: `Boolean`

Whether to add an `Import-Module` line for this module to every profile
file managed by `windowspowershell::config` (see `manage_profiles` /
`manage_pwsh_profile` on the main class). Defaults to `true`, but the
import is often unnecessary: the module is under the machine-wide module
directory and exports its functions by name, so PowerShell auto-loads it on
first use, while the profile import adds to the startup time of every
session. Keep it when the aliases or variables the module defines are
needed from the start of the session. A failed import prints a warning.

Default value: `true`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--module--source"></a>`source`

Data type: `Optional[String[1]]`

Optional Puppet file source bulk-deploying every script under it straight
into `Functions`, one recursive, **purging** copy preserving the source
tree -- the "dynamic" way to build a module: drop a new `.ps1` under that
source directory (optionally in a sub-folder) and it ships on the next
Puppet run, with no Puppet code change and no per-script resource. Because
this copy purges, it takes over the *whole* `Functions` directory: do not
mix it with `windowspowershell::script` resources naming the same module,
since this copy would remove what they manage (and vice versa) on the
next run. Left `undef` (the default), nothing is copied in bulk and
`Functions` is only ever populated by individual `windowspowershell::script`
resources, which remains the right choice for dynamic content (e.g. a
template).

Default value: `undef`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--module--purge_versions"></a>`purge_versions`

Data type: `Boolean`

Whether to remove versions of the module other than the one in `version`.
Co-managing one modulename from both `windowspowershell::module` and
`windowspowershell::external_module` requires `purge_versions => false` on
one side, or each purge removes the other side's version.
The purge reuses the same numeric comparison as
`windowspowershell::external_module`: missing segments count as zero, so
pin `2.3` also keeps a `2.3.0` folder left behind by an earlier layout,
and a folder that does not parse as `[version]` is kept, never purged.

Default value: `true`

### <a name="windowspowershell--script"></a>`windowspowershell::script`

The script is written under the target module's `Functions` directory and
notifies that module's shared manifest-regeneration Exec, so it is exported
on the next PowerShell session. Removing it is the same resource with
`ensure => absent`.

#### Examples

##### 

```puppet
windowspowershell::script { 'Get-WUParams':
  modulename => 'Acme',
  folder     => 'Windowsupdate',
  content    => template('windowsupdate/windowspowershell/Get-WUParams.ps1.erb'),
}
```

##### Retire a script that is no longer shipped

```puppet
windowspowershell::script { 'Get-OldThing':
  modulename => 'Acme',
  ensure     => absent,
}
```

* [`ensure`](#-windowspowershell--script--ensure)
* [`scriptname`](#-windowspowershell--script--scriptname)
* [`folder`](#-windowspowershell--script--folder)
* [`content`](#-windowspowershell--script--content)
* [`source`](#-windowspowershell--script--source)

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--script--modulename"></a>`modulename`

Data type: `Windowspowershell::Name`

Name of the in-house module (a `windowspowershell::module`
resource) this script is deployed into. Mandatory: there is no default
module any more, so every script has to say where it is going. A module
named here that was never declared explicitly is created with every
default (see `windowspowershell::module`).

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--script--ensure"></a>`ensure`

Data type: `Enum['present', 'absent']`

Whether the script should be present or absent.

Default value: `'present'`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--script--scriptname"></a>`scriptname`

Data type: `Windowspowershell::Name`

Base name of the script, without the `.ps1` extension. Defaults to the
resource title. This is also the name of the exported PowerShell function.
A trailing `.ps1`/`.psm1` is refused: the module appends `.ps1` itself, so
`Get-Foo.ps1` would deploy `Get-Foo.ps1.ps1` exporting a broken function
name. Dots elsewhere stay legitimate (`Get-Example.v2`).

Default value: `$name`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--script--folder"></a>`folder`

Data type: `Optional[Windowspowershell::Name]`

Optional sub-folder under `Functions`, to group scripts by domain.

Default value: `undef`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--script--content"></a>`content`

Data type: `Optional[String[1]]`

Literal content of the script. Mutually exclusive with `source`.

Default value: `undef`

##### <a name="-windowspowershell--script--source"></a>`source`

Data type: `Optional[String[1]]`

Puppet file source for the script. Mutually exclusive with `content`.

Default value: `undef`

## Data types

### <a name="Windowspowershell--Externalmoduleensure"></a>`Windowspowershell::Externalmoduleensure`

Desired state of an external PowerShell module, mirroring the `package` type: a
literal version pins that exact version, `present` accepts any version, and
`absent` removes every version installed under the machine-wide (`AllUsers`)
module directory and unregisters the module from PowerShellGet.

`latest` is deliberately absent. Resolving it requires a `Find-Module` call
on every Puppet run, and it lets two nodes end up on different versions
depending on the day they last ran.

Alias of `Variant[Enum['present', 'absent'], Windowspowershell::Version]`

### <a name="Windowspowershell--Moduleversion"></a>`Windowspowershell::Moduleversion`

A PowerShell module version that New-ModuleManifest can actually write: two to
four dot-separated numbers of at most nine digits each. That is the shape
PowerShell's `[version]` type and its `-ModuleVersion` parameter accept -- a
major and a minor component at minimum, every component within Int32 -- so the
cast it performs cannot fail at Exec runtime.

A single number such as `1` consists only of digits, so it slips past
Windowspowershell::Version, and casting it to `[version]` throws. This alias
rules that out at compile time instead.

Leading zeros are still allowed, so `01.02` passes here and PowerShell reports
the module as `1.2` while the folder keeps its `01.02` name.

Alias of `Pattern[/\A\d{1,9}(\.\d{1,9}){1,3}\z/]`

### <a name="Windowspowershell--Name"></a>`Windowspowershell::Name`

A single path component: a script, folder or module name.

Three properties are guaranteed, and the module relies on all three:

* It names one component and cannot escape its parent directory. The path
  separators are excluded, and a name made only of dots is refused along with
  every other name ending in a dot.
* It is safe to interpolate into a single-quoted PowerShell string. What can
  end such a string is the ASCII apostrophe and the typographic single quotes
  PowerShell also treats as quote characters (U+2018 to U+201B) -- the
  backtick and `$` are literal inside it -- so excluding those is what keeps
  the generated scripts free of injection.
* It is not a Windows reserved device name. CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1-9 and
  LPT1-9 are refused case-insensitively, with or without an extension;
  spaces between the stem and the extension do not save it either.

The remaining exclusions are what Windows itself refuses in a file name: the
reserved characters, control characters, a trailing dot or space, and more
than 255 characters in a single path component.

Alias of `Pattern[/\A(?!(?i:CON|PRN|AUX|NUL|COM[1-9]|LPT[1-9])[ ]*(?:\..*)?\z)[^\\\/:*?"<>|'\u2018-\u201B\x00-\x1F]{0,254}[^\\\/:*?"<>|'\u2018-\u201B\x00-\x1F. ]\z/]`

### <a name="Windowspowershell--Proxyurl"></a>`Windowspowershell::Proxyurl`

A proxy URL that is safe to embed in a single-quoted PowerShell string.

Stdlib::HTTPUrl accepts anything after the scheme, an apostrophe included. The
proxy is interpolated between single quotes in the generated scripts, which
the agent runs as SYSTEM, so this alias keeps the `http://` or `https://`
scheme requirement and refuses whatever could end the quoted string: the ASCII
apostrophe, the typographic single quotes that PowerShell also treats as
quote characters (U+2018 to U+201B), control characters and whitespace.

Credentials embedded in the URL (`http://user:pass@host`) still match. That
form is deprecated in favour of `proxy_credential`, but it is not refused here.

Alias of `Pattern[/\A(?i:https?):\/\/[^'\u2018-\u201B\x00-\x1F\s]+\z/]`

### <a name="Windowspowershell--Psstring"></a>`Windowspowershell::Psstring`

Free text that ends up inside a single-quoted PowerShell string, such as the
author or company written into the module manifest.

Unlike Windowspowershell::Name this is not a path component, so spaces,
dots and most punctuation are fine. Only what could break out of the quoted
string is refused: the apostrophe, the typographic single quotes PowerShell
also treats as quote characters (U+2018 to U+201B), and control characters.

Alias of `Pattern[/\A[^'\u2018-\u201B\x00-\x1F]{1,255}\z/]`

### <a name="Windowspowershell--Reponame"></a>`Windowspowershell::Reponame`

Name of a PowerShell repository, as registered by `Register-PSRepository`
and passed to `Install-Module -Repository`.

Deliberately narrower than what PowerShellGet would accept: the value is
interpolated into a single-quoted PowerShell string, so it is restricted to
the characters real repository names use -- `PSGallery`, `Internal-Repo`,
`nuget.local` -- and nothing that could end that string.

Alias of `Pattern[/\A[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}\z/]`

### <a name="Windowspowershell--Rootpath"></a>`Windowspowershell::Rootpath`

The machine-wide PowerShell module root, e.g. the parent of every in-house
module folder this class lays out.

It composes two constraints that Puppet, lacking an intersection type, cannot
express separately:

* The shape of an absolute Windows path, exactly as Stdlib::Windowspath
  anchors it at the start: a drive letter, a UNC share, or a `\\?\` prefix.
* Safety inside a single-quoted PowerShell string. `$module_root` feeds
  `$module_path`, which is interpolated between single quotes in the manifest
  template, so the apostrophe and the typographic single quotes PowerShell
  also treats as quote characters (U+2018 to U+201B) -- the only characters
  able to end such a string -- and the control characters are refused, here
  and inside the UNC server and share segments too.

The paths derived from it are safe by construction. Other values that reach a
PowerShell string, such as the proxy URL, are constrained by their own type
(see Windowspowershell::Proxyurl).

Alias of `Pattern[/\A(?:[A-Za-z]:[\\\/]|[\\\/][\\\/][^\\\/'\u2018-\u201B\x00-\x1F]+[\\\/][^\\\/'\u2018-\u201B\x00-\x1F]+|[\\\/][\\\/]\?[\\\/][^\\\/'\u2018-\u201B\x00-\x1F]+)[^'\u2018-\u201B\x00-\x1F]*\z/]`

### <a name="Windowspowershell--Version"></a>`Windowspowershell::Version`

A PowerShell module version: one to four dot-separated numbers of at most
nine digits each.

Deliberately looser than Windowspowershell::Moduleversion, which requires at
least two components. This type serves windowspowershell::external_module,
whose version reaches PowerShellGet's Install-Module -RequiredVersion as a
plain string and is accepted there as it stands. A single-component pin
such as `2` is therefore still accepted here; the profile fragment
normalises it to `2.0` because Import-Module -RequiredVersion is typed
[version], which needs at least major.minor.

Each component is still limited to nine digits, like Moduleversion: every
component is parsed as an Int32 by System.Version, so a tenth digit would
overflow at Exec runtime instead of failing the catalogue at compile time.

Being digits and dots only, it is also safe to interpolate into a
single-quoted PowerShell string and into a directory name.

Alias of `Pattern[/\A\d{1,9}(\.\d{1,9}){0,3}\z/]`
